prop: Every observation in this memo was taken against the tetel worktree at commit 86f8c6e263004a0c7cfc78b5cc0f0ea6d0ea88ac on branch verify-jev-eval, with no tracked path modified or staged; the one untracked path, scratchpad_backup_jps.ts at the repository root, is unrelated to this design.

Jev cannot perform the check leg. The check leg's product is a `Finding` whose `clause` is the author's own words and whose evidence is a quoted span, returned as text by an OpenAI-style chat call; TypeSafe's endpoint returns, for a map of typed questions, an object whose only top-level keys are `answers`, `model` and `usage`, where each answer is a probability, a choice among the request's own keys, or a score index — and the only strings in it are the request's own labels echoed back. Every design below therefore keeps an LLM on OpenRouter for the check leg and gives Jev only legs whose answer is a choice.

As the refuter on `fact`, Jev performs within the range of the two LLM refuters measured on the same 16 adjudicated `contradicts` findings, at under a hundredth of their cost: Jev (3-draw majority) keeps 8 of 10 true catches at 80% precision, against Sonnet's 8 of 10 at 89% and Gemini's 10 of 10 at 77%; one Jev draw cost $0.0018 for all 16 findings (README: $0.00011 a finding, against $0.0228 and $0.0184), with a median latency of 0.69 seconds.

A Jev gate in front of the check leg separates the subjects worth checking from the rest on `fact` and `claim` but not on `prose`, and only when asked which unit disagrees rather than whether anything does. Asked of the whole note (`whole`) it saves -1% on `fact` and 8% on `claim`. Asked as one `choice` over the note's sentences plus NONE, with each sentence also classified and only the current share counted (`pick_cls`), it skips 60% of `fact` subjects with none of the 12 adjudicated defects skipped, a 58% net saving; asked as one `choice` over clauses (`pick_clause`), it skips 27% of `claim` subjects with none of the 10 adjudicated-correct warnings skipped, a 21% net saving, and removes 4 of the 13 adjudicated false alarms. On `prose` no variant exceeds AUC 0.69. Each threshold sits 0.05 below the lowest-scoring positive — 0.50 on `fact`, 0.58 on `claim` — and was fitted on those same 12 and 10 positives, with nothing held out.

On the `claim` verb, replacing the LLM classify call with Jev's labels leaves the check leg's output equal in quality at 39% of the cost: over the same 125 claims, three draws each, the same LLM check flags 11 adjudicated-correct warnings under either classifier, with 16 wrong under Jev's labels against 15 under the LLM's, for $1.588 against $4.068. The LLM classify call alone costs $0.0054 a draw of the $0.011 the two calls cost together. Jev's arm flags 8 supports-only claims against the LLM arm's 6, which straddles the design's steering-hazard line of 7; the same LLM configuration flagged 4 in August, so the difference is inside draw-to-draw variation, but it is unresolved. The classify comparison covers the `claim` verb only.

When code proposes the literal candidates and the shipped filters run unchanged, Jev judging them matches the LLM literal leg on the same 88 claims at a sixth of the cost: 82% precision and 18% recall (9 of 11 flagged claims later needed work) against the LLM's 80% and 16% (8 of 10), at $0.00023 a draw against $0.00132, with 17 of 21 literals raised in every draw against 6 of 29. Added to the check leg alone, either literal leg raises the supports-only claims flagged from 4 of 38 to 5 or 6, over the 11.3% steering-hazard line; behind the Jev claim gate, check plus Jev literals flags 4 of 38 and 20 of 50 claims that needed work, against 18 for the check alone. That joint figure is computed against the August check-leg flags, not a joint run.

The name `jev-latest` is an alias the endpoint resolves to a versioned model — `jev-1.13.0` on the day this memo was written — and reports in each response's `model` field; none of the benchmark's Jev result files recorded the resolved version, so every number above is tied to an alias whose target is not on record.

The comment above `run()` in src/verify.rs says the ratio between `split`'s two calls "is measured nowhere" and implies that the classify call — which "carries the claim text alone" — is the cheap one. On the `claim` verb it is now measured, and the classify call is about half the cost of a `split` verification: $0.0054 a draw on the draws where it ran alone, against $0.011 for classify and check together.

A Jev gate in front of the check leg is worth having on `fact` and `claim` but not on `prose`, and what makes it worth having is asking which unit disagrees rather than whether anything does. Asked of the whole note (`whole`) it saves -1% on `fact` and 8% on `claim`. Asked as one `choice` over the note's sentences plus NONE, with each sentence also classified and only the current share counted (`pick_cls`), it skips 60% of `fact` subjects with none of the 12 adjudicated defects skipped, a 58% net saving; asked as one `choice` over clauses (`pick_clause`), it skips 27% of `claim` subjects with none of the 10 adjudicated-correct warnings skipped, a 21% net saving, and removes 4 of the 13 adjudicated false alarms. On `prose` no variant exceeds AUC 0.69. Each threshold sits 0.05 below the lowest-scoring positive — 0.50 on `fact`, 0.58 on `claim` — and was fitted on those same 12 and 10 positives, with nothing held out.
why: The verifier's contradicts finding is right: the whole-note gate still separates on claim (AUC 0.69, 8% net), so "only when asked which unit disagrees" contradicts the claim's own figure. Narrowed to what the capture shows: asking which unit disagrees is what turns a marginal gate into a useful one.

prop: Read per draw rather than per claim, the supports-only claims flagged do not separate the two classifiers: 24 of 185 draws (13.0%) with Jev's labels against 22 of 185 (11.9%) with the LLM's, a difference of two draws — while the same LLM classify-and-check configuration moved from 18 of 183 (9.8%) in August to 22 of 185 today. Per draw, today's shipped configuration itself flags supports-only claims above the 11.3% steering-hazard line, so the line is a question about the check leg as it now behaves, not about which classifier feeds it.

Decision — routing and credential. A model value whose vendor half is exactly `typesafe` is sent to TypeSafe's endpoint (a second constant beside `ENDPOINT`, https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone) with a credential read only from the environment variable TYPESAFE_API_KEY, on the same terms `KEY_VARS` states for OpenRouter's: never a config key, never written. Every other value keeps going to OpenRouter unchanged. `is_model_name` already accepts `typesafe/jev-1.13.0`, so the routing needs no new value syntax. `verify.model` refuses a `typesafe/` value at `config set`, through a new `Accepts` variant, because the check leg must be an LLM and a refusal at `config set` can never suppress a mint, where a refusal at mint time would.

Decision — one new key, `verify.typed_model`, not a `verify.provider` and not one key per leg. A provider key would describe a switch that cannot exist: whatever it is set to, the check leg stays on OpenRouter. One key per leg would each have to be printed in every response and each have to earn its place, for legs that never run apart from a per-verb table. Unset, the verifier is byte-identical to today. Set to a `typesafe/` value, it enables the typed legs that a per-verb table in source names for each verb — the same status `classify_system_for` already gives the classify prompt — and every response prints it as `typed_model`, beside the version the endpoint resolved it to.

Decision — the per-verb table carries only what was measured on that verb. `fact`: a gate asked as a `choice` over sentences with per-sentence classification (`pick_cls`), skipping below 0.45; classify stays on the LLM, because the Jev port of the classify prompt `fact` shares with `claim` was never run on `fact`; the literal leg's judgement stays on the LLM, because `literal_findings` takes no verb and Jev's literal judgement was measured on claims only. `claim`: a gate asked as a `choice` over clauses (`pick_clause`), skipping below 0.53; classify by Jev, over clauses cut outside brackets and code spans, a clause counting as current at P(current) >= 0.4; the literal leg judged by Jev when `verify.literals` is on. `prose`: no typed leg, since no gate presentation separated and prose is off by default. The two gates are different presentations, not one gate with two thresholds: `pick_cls` saves 7% on `claim` against `pick_clause`'s 21%.

Jev cannot perform the check leg. The check leg's product is a `Finding` whose `clause` is meant to quote the author and whose evidence is a quoted span, returned as text by an OpenAI-style chat call. The response TypeSafe's endpoint returned to a request carrying one of each question type had exactly three top-level keys, `answers`, `model` and `usage`, and each answer was an object carrying a probability, a choice among the request's own keys, or a score index, with its probabilities; the only text in it was the question type names and the request's own labels echoed back. Nothing in that shape can carry a clause, a reason or a quotation, so every design below keeps an LLM on OpenRouter for the check leg and gives Jev only legs whose answer is a choice.
why: Four verifier findings, all fair: the clause is meant to be the author's words and is flagged (clause_quoted) when it is not; "only top-level keys" rested on one response; each answer is an object carrying a probability/choice/score, not a bare value; and the response also carries the question type names. Narrowed to what the capture shows; the conclusion does not depend on any of the four.

prop: Decision — what the gate does to a verification. The gate asks its question first, of the subject's text and evidence alone, before any classify call, which is how it was measured. Below the verb's threshold, no classify and no check call is made and the verification reports a new status, `gated`, never `ok` with an empty findings list: `Status` exists so that nothing empty passes for a clean result. The literal leg, when on, still runs on a gated subject, since it answers a different question and the measured join shows literals-always-run at 20 of 50 needed-work claims flagged against 19 with literals gated, both at 4 of 38 sound. A gate that fails — transport, timeout, an unreadable reply — never skips: the check runs, and the response carries `gate_incomplete` the way it carries `literals_incomplete` today. The gate's probability is never shown to the author; `Finding` carries no confidence score by design, and a verification should not either.

Decision — `verify.literals` stays off by default, `typed_model` or not. The only joint figure for the literal leg with the gate — 20 of 50 needed-work claims and 4 of 38 sound claims flagged — was computed against the August check-leg flags with the LLM classifier, not from a run of the configuration that would ship, which also has Jev classify on `claim`. `verify_literals` is documented as off precisely because defaulting it on "would fold an unmeasured check into the numbers `docs/verify.md` quotes", and that reason applies unchanged. Flipping the default is owed one joint run of gate, Jev classify, check and Jev literals over the same claims.

Each typed leg ships with the presentation it was measured with, including its splitter, because the numbers belong to the presentation and not to the model. The `fact` gate (`pick_cls`) splits into sentences, asks one `choice` over them plus NONE and one CURRENT/PROPOSED/ARGUMENT `choice` per sentence, and scores the sum of each sentence's pick probability times its P(CURRENT). The `claim` gate (`pick_clause`) cuts every sentence at every `,` `;` `:` or dash, with no bracket awareness, asks one `choice` over the clauses plus NONE, and scores 1 - P(NONE). Jev classify on `claim` cuts clauses only outside brackets and code spans. Both gates put the subject's text before its evidence; both carry NOT_A_DISAGREEMENT, ported from CHECK_SYSTEM, in NONE's criterion. A port that "improves" any of these — one splitter for both, a shared score — is an unmeasured configuration.

Decision — the refuter. `verify.refuter_model` accepts a `typesafe/` value, answered as one `choice` over CORRECT, WRONG and UNCLEAR with REFUTE_SYSTEM's own criteria, the measured port; only WRONG drops, unchanged. The default refuter stays the LLM it is: Jev's refuter numbers cover `fact`'s `contradicts` findings only. The self-refutation guard in `refute_findings`, which today compares the refuter only against `verify.model`, extends to `verify.typed_model`: when both name the same model, the refuter is not run over `unevidenced` findings that model judged, and `tel.detail` says so as the existing branch does. A refuter call that fails keeps its finding, as today, and the response names the failure as `refuter_incomplete`, so that unrefuted findings do not reach an author under a printed `refuter_model`.

Decision — the version. Every threshold in the per-verb table was fitted to one version's probabilities, and the benchmark recorded only the alias. The code names, beside the table, the version the endpoint returned for `jev-latest` on the day of measurement — `typesafe/jev-1.13.0`, recorded from a spike, not from the runs themselves — reads the resolved `model` from every reply, prints it in every response, and adds `typed_model_unmeasured` when it differs from that constant. That flag fails nothing; it states which numbers no longer describe what ran, in the same posture as `deterministic: false`.

Decision — credential and budget. With a `typesafe/` value set and TYPESAFE_API_KEY absent, the verification reports `unauthorized` and the `missing` diagnostic gains an arm naming TYPESAFE_API_KEY; it never falls back to running the LLM legs while printing a typed model it did not use. Typed legs get their own per-leg budget constant instead of `DEFAULT_MS_PER_LEG`'s 60 seconds, which `expected_calls` multiplies into the default timeout: one Jev draw over 16 findings had a median latency of 0.69 seconds and a maximum of 1.01, so three typed legs at 60 seconds each would quadruple a budget for calls that take about a second.

The supports-only claims flagged do not separate the two classifiers by more than the check leg's own drift between runs. The steering-hazard line is defined over claims — 7 of 62 — and counted that way Jev's arm flags 8 and the LLM's 6, on either side of it. Counted per draw, the two differ by two draws: 24 of 185 (13.0%) with Jev's labels against 22 of 185 (11.9%) with the LLM's; while the same LLM classify-and-check configuration moved from 18 of 183 (9.8%) in August to 22 of 185 today. The line's verdict on Jev classify therefore rests on a difference smaller than the variation of the configuration it is compared against, and is not settled by these runs.
why: The verifier's finding exposed a real error: the steering-hazard line is defined per claim, and applying it per draw reinterpreted its unit. Counted per claim the LLM arm is under the line (6) and the Jev arm over (8). What the per-draw view does establish — that the two classifiers differ by less than the configuration's own drift — is kept; the claim that today's shipped configuration is over the line is withdrawn.

prop: Decision — `verify.literals` stays off by default, `typed_model` or not. The only joint figure for Jev's literal leg behind the gate — 20 of 50 needed-work claims and 4 of 38 sound claims flagged — joins Jev's literal judgements to the check leg's August flags, and those flags came from a check fed by the LLM's classify call, not Jev's. No run has measured the configuration that would ship, which also has Jev classify on `claim`. `verify_literals` is documented as off precisely because defaulting it on "would fold an unmeasured check into the numbers `docs/verify.md` quotes", and that reason applies unchanged. Flipping the default is owed one joint run of gate, Jev classify, check and Jev literals over the same claims.
why: A verifier finding read "with the LLM classifier" as describing the literal judgement, which in that figure was Jev's. The phrase describes the check-leg flags the literals were joined to. Made explicit.

prop: Decision — `verify.typed_model` is unset by default, and becomes the default only after one joint run of gate, Jev classify, check and Jev literals on the `claim` corpus shows supports-only claims flagged under 7 of 62, the design's own line, counted per claim. Until then the typed legs reach only an author who set the key: the unsettled comparison of the two classifiers against that line is not a reason to withhold an opt-in configuration whose correct warnings matched the LLM's at 39% of the cost, and it is a reason not to make it what every mint runs.

Rejected, each on its own measurement: a gate asked of the whole note (`whole`: -1% net on `fact`, 8% on `claim`); gate criteria rewritten for recall, dropping CHECK_SYSTEM's exclusions (`pick_recall`: 44% net on `fact` against `pick`'s 52%, and AUC 0.59 on `prose` against 0.65); the capture placed before the author's text (`pick_evfirst`: 20% net on `fact`); and a gate on `prose`, where no variant exceeds AUC 0.69. Also rejected without a run: surfacing any Jev probability to the author as a confidence, which `Finding` excludes by design.

The implementation surface is src/verify.rs and src/config.rs, plus docs/verify.md. The declared `Status` is the verifier's enum at src/verify.rs:120 — a different `pub enum Status`, a ledger row's, sits at src/model.rs:46 and is not touched. `run()` in src/verify.rs is modified too, to place the gate before classify and route classify by verb; it is not declared as a target, because a whole-worktree census of the symbol `run` would match nearly every file. Four pieces of prose become false or stay false under this change and move in the same commit: `ENDPOINT`'s doc ("the only endpoint this module knows"), the comment above `run()` that calls the classify/check cost ratio "measured nowhere", `verify.literals`' summary, which already says a failed literal call "fails the whole verification" although `run()` no longer lets it, and docs/verify.md's settings table, which gains `verify.typed_model`.

Invariants, each paired with the revert that must turn its test red; demonstration is owed when the code exists. (1) With `verify.typed_model` unset, a verification makes the same calls in the same order and prints the same fields as today — revert: default `typed_model` to a typesafe value. (2) A subject scored below its verb's gate threshold reports status `gated`, and no classify or check call is made — revert: return `ok` with empty findings. (3) A gate call that fails runs the check, and the response carries `gate_incomplete` — revert: treat a failed gate as a skip. (4) `config set verify.model typesafe/jev-1.13.0` is refused — revert: accept any model name for `verify.model`. (5) With `typed_model` and `refuter_model` naming the same model, the refuter is not run over `unevidenced` findings that model judged, and `tel.detail` says so — revert: compare the refuter against `verify.model` only. (6) With a `typesafe/` value set and TYPESAFE_API_KEY absent, the status is `unauthorized` and the message names TYPESAFE_API_KEY — revert: fall back to the LLM legs. (7) A reply whose resolved `model` differs from the measured constant adds `typed_model_unmeasured` — revert: compare against the configured alias. (8) `fact` never runs Jev classify or Jev literal judgement, and `prose` runs no typed leg — revert: one table row for every verb.

Confined it to `fact`, the verb it was measured on, and named the mechanism — a verb parameter on refute_findings. Also recorded the attack that failed: the self-refutation guard's `unevidenced` scope is exactly right, since that is the only kind literal_findings emits.

prop: Decision — credential and budget. With a `typesafe/` value set on a key whose leg this verb's table row actually runs, and TYPESAFE_API_KEY absent, the verification reports `unauthorized` and the `missing` diagnostic gains an arm naming TYPESAFE_API_KEY; it never falls back to running the LLM legs while printing a typed model it did not use. The condition is the leg that will run, not the presence of a `typesafe/` string anywhere: a `typesafe/` refuter on `claim`, which that row does not use, must not turn a leg documented as one that cannot fail a verification into a whole-verification failure. Typed legs get their own per-leg budget constant instead of `DEFAULT_MS_PER_LEG`'s 60 seconds: one Jev draw over 16 findings had a median latency of 0.69 seconds and a maximum of 1.01, so three typed legs at 60 seconds each would quadruple a budget for calls that take about a second. The mechanism as it stands cannot express that. `settings()` computes one `timeout_ms` as a single product, `DEFAULT_MS_PER_LEG * expected_calls(&approach, literals, refuter.is_some())`, and `expected_calls` returns one `u32` from those three arguments — one constant times one count cannot describe a run that is LLM legs at 60 seconds plus typed legs at about one. So `expected_calls` returns a count per provider and the timeout becomes the sum of two products; and because the per-verb table makes the typed count verb-dependent while `settings()` has no verb in scope, the verb reaches the place the count is computed.
why: Attack pass a1, finding 5 (verified at src/verify.rs:391-400 and 2377-2384). The decision named a budget the mechanism cannot express — a single constant times a single count — and left `unauthorized` keyed on "a typesafe value set" without saying which key, which would let an unused refuter value fail a whole verification. prop: Decision — `verify.typed_model` is unset by default, and becomes the default only after one joint run of gate, Jev classify, check and Jev literals on the `claim` corpus. prop: A Jev gate in front of the check leg is worth having on `fact` and `claim` but not on `prose`, and what makes it worth having is asking which unit disagrees rather than whether anything does. Asked of the whole note (`whole`) it saves -1% on `fact` and 8% on `claim`. Asked as one `choice` over the note's sentences plus NONE, with each sentence also classified and only the current share counted (`pick_cls`), it skips 60% of `fact` subjects with none of the 12 adjudicated defects skipped, a 58% net saving; asked as one `choice` over clauses (`pick_clause`), it skips 27% of `claim` subjects with none of the 10 adjudicated-correct warnings skipped, a 21% net saving, and removes 4 of the 13 adjudicated false alarms. On `prose` no variant exceeds AUC 0.69. The lowest-scoring positive is 0.50 on `fact` (tet56 F29) and 0.58 on `claim` (tet56 C3), and each threshold sits 0.05 below it — 0.45 and 0.53, the values the per-verb table carries. Both were fitted on those same 12 and 10 positives, with nothing held out.
why: Attack pass a1, finding 7, re-derived this session: "Each threshold sits 0.05 below the lowest-scoring positive — 0.50 on `fact`, 0.58 on `claim`" attached the two numbers to the threshold rather than to the lowest positive, so the sentence read alone builds a gate 0.05 too high on both verbs. score_gate_variants.py gives lowest positives of 0.50 and 0.58 and thresholds of 0.45 and 0.53, which is what C12 says.

prop: Decision — `verify.literals` stays off by default, `typed_model` or not. The only joint figures for Jev's literal leg behind the gate — 20 of 50 needed-work claims flagged with literals always run, 19 with literals gated too, 4 of 38 sound claims either way — join Jev's literal judgements to the check leg's August flags, and those flags came from a check fed by the LLM's classify call, not Jev's. No run has measured the configuration that would ship, which also has Jev classify on `claim`. `verify_literals` is documented as off precisely because defaulting it on "would fold an unmeasured check into the numbers `docs/verify.md` quotes", and that reason applies unchanged. Flipping the default is owed the same joint run C19 owes, over the same claims, and judged on the same rate: the literals-gated arm is the one that matters, since a gated subject emits no findings at all.
why: Follows C13's revision: the literal leg no longer runs on a gated subject, so the always-run arm is no longer a shipping candidate and the joint run must be judged on the gated arm. Also ties the owed run to C19's, which is the same run, and to the rate rather than the count.

prop: Invariants, each paired with the revert that must turn its test red; demonstration is owed when the code exists. (1) With no `typesafe/` value on any verify key, a verification makes the same calls in the same order and prints the same fields as today — revert: default `typed_model` to a typesafe value. Stated over the keys and not over `typed_model` alone, because routing follows the model value's vendor half and `verify.refuter_model` accepts a `typesafe/` value today; an invariant written over `typed_model` would go green while a typesafe refuter was already calling TypeSafe. (2) A subject scored below its verb's gate threshold reports status `gated`, and no classify, check or literal call is made — revert: return `ok` with empty findings. (3) A gate call that fails runs the check, and the response carries `gate_incomplete` — revert: treat a failed gate as a skip. (4) `config set verify.model typesafe/jev-1.13.0` is refused — revert: accept any model name for `verify.model`. (5) With `typed_model` and `refuter_model` naming the same model, the refuter is not run over `unevidenced` findings that model judged, and `tel.detail` says so — revert: compare the refuter against `verify.model` only. (6) With a `typesafe/` value on a key this verb's row actually runs and TYPESAFE_API_KEY absent, the status is `unauthorized` and the message names TYPESAFE_API_KEY; with a `typesafe/` value only on a key this verb's row does not run, the verification is unaffected — revert: fall back to the LLM legs, and separately, key `unauthorized` on any typesafe value anywhere. (7) A reply whose resolved `model` differs from the measured constant adds `typed_model_unmeasured` — revert: compare against the configured alias. (8) Each verb runs only its own row, over every typed leg including the refuter: `fact` runs no Jev classify and no Jev literal judgement, `claim` runs no typed refuter even with a `typesafe/` refuter_model set, and `prose` runs no typed leg at all — revert: one table row for every verb, and separately, drop the verb parameter from `refute_findings` so a typesafe refuter runs on every verb.
why: Attack pass a1, finding 1, verified: invariants (1) and (8) were both false from one construction — `verify.refuter_model = typesafe/...` with `typed_model` unset routes to TypeSafe, and `run()` calls `refute_findings` for every verb with no verb guard. Each invariant's own revert test would have passed while the property it advertised was false. (1) is now stated over the keys, (8) over every typed leg with the refuter named, (2) gains the literal call per C13, and (6) gains the negative half that stops an unused refuter value failing a verification.

prop: This memo's observations were taken against the tetel worktree on branch verify-jev-eval, pinned at commit 86f8c6e263004a0c7cfc78b5cc0f0ea6d0ea88ac, and the tree was not clean. prop: Decision — the refuter. `verify.refuter_model` accepts a `typesafe/` value — it already does, and no new `Accepts` variant is proposed to stop it — answered as one `choice` over CORRECT, WRONG and UNCLEAR with REFUTE_SYSTEM's own criteria, the measured port; only WRONG drops, unchanged. A `typesafe/` refuter runs on `fact` alone, and the reason is a measurement rather than an absence of one: Jev's refuter was also run on `prose`, over 44 adjudicated findings of which 28 are `contradicts`, and there it keeps 13 of 44 at 31% precision on a single draw and 12 at 33% on the 3-draw majority, losing 2 of 6 true catches — against 8 of 10 at 80% on `fact`. `claim` is the verb with no Jev refuter run at all, and gets no typed refuter for that reason. `refute_findings` gains the verb it does not take today, so that a `typesafe/` refuter set on any other verb is not used and the response says so rather than silently running it. The self-refutation guard in `refute_findings`, which today compares the refuter only against `verify.model`, extends to `verify.typed_model`: when both name the same model, the refuter is not run over `unevidenced` findings that model judged, and `tel.detail` says so as the existing branch does. The guard is correctly scoped to `unevidenced` findings, because those are exactly the findings `literal_findings` emits — a Jev refuter judging `contradicts` findings from an LLM check leg is not refuting itself. A refuter call that fails keeps its finding, as today, and the response names the failure as `refuter_incomplete`, so that unrefuted findings do not reach an author under a printed `refuter_model`.

prop: Decision — the per-verb table carries only what was measured on that verb, and it covers every typed leg including the refuter. `fact`: a gate asked as a `choice` over sentences with per-sentence classification (`pick_cls`), skipping below 0.45; classify stays on the LLM, because the Jev port of the classify prompt `fact` shares with `claim` was never run on `fact`; the literal leg's judgement stays on the LLM, because `literal_findings` takes no verb and Jev's literal judgement was measured on claims only; a `typesafe/` refuter is permitted, this being the verb whose Jev refuter numbers are good rather than merely present. `claim`: a gate asked as a `choice` over clauses (`pick_clause`), skipping below 0.53; classify by Jev, over clauses cut outside brackets and code spans, a clause counting as current at P(current) >= 0.4; the literal leg judged by Jev when `verify.literals` is on; the refuter stays an LLM, this being the one verb with no Jev refuter run at all. `prose`: no typed leg, since no gate presentation separated, prose is off by default, and the Jev refuter was measured there at 31-33% precision against 80% on `fact`. The two gates are different presentations, not one gate with two thresholds: `pick_cls` saves 7% on `claim` against `pick_clause`'s 21%. prop: Jev cannot perform the check leg. The check leg's product is a list of `Finding`s, each with a `clause` meant to quote the author and a quoted evidence span, returned as text by an OpenAI-style chat call — that half is checkable in the tree, and `Finding` carries no confidence field anywhere, `payload()` included. The other half is a live observation this memo made and nothing in the worktree corroborates: the response TypeSafe's endpoint returned to a request carrying one of each question type had exactly three top-level keys, `answers`, `model` and `usage`, and each answer was an object carrying a probability, a choice among the request's own keys, or a score index, with its probabilities; the only text in it was the resolved model name, the question type names and the request's own labels echoed back. No harness stores a raw response — `jev.ask()` keeps only `answers` and `usage` — so the witness is this memo's own capture and not a file anyone can re-read. Nothing in that shape can carry a clause, a reason or a quotation, so every design below keeps an LLM on OpenRouter for the check leg and gives Jev only legs whose answer is a choice.
why: Grounding pass k1 qualified C2: the response-shape observation has no on-disk witness, because jev.ask() discards everything but `answers` and `usage`, so a reader cannot check it from the tree. The claim is unchanged in substance but now says which half rests on this memo's own live call.

prop: The name `jev-latest` is an alias the endpoint resolves to a versioned model and reports in each response's `model` field, and on the day this memo was written it resolved to `jev-1.13.0`. That resolution is witnessed only by this memo's own live call: every Jev harness writes the alias into its result file as `"model": jev.MODEL`, `jev.ask()` discards the reply's own `model` field, and no file in the worktree contains the string `jev-1.` at all. So every number in this memo is tied to an alias whose target is not on record anywhere a reader can check, and the design's response to that is in C17 — read the resolved version from every reply rather than trust the constant.
why: Grounding pass k1: the second half (no benchmark file records the version) is strongly witnessed, but the alias-resolution half rests on the live call alone. Said so, and pointed at the decision that exists because of it.

prop: Decision — the version. Every threshold in the per-verb table was fitted to one version's probabilities, and no benchmark file records which version answered — where a file names a Jev model at all, it names the alias `jev-latest`, and the string `jev-1.` appears nowhere in the worktree. The code names, beside the table, the version the endpoint returned for `jev-latest` on the day of measurement, `typesafe/jev-1.13.0`, reads the resolved `model` from every reply, prints it in every response, and adds `typed_model_unmeasured` when it differs from that constant. The constant is the weakest thing in this design: it comes from a spike whose response was not recorded, not from the measurement runs, so nothing in the tree can confirm that the numbers were produced by the version the flag will compare against. The flag is worth having anyway, because it is the only mechanism that can ever notice the alias moving, and it is worth having exactly because it fails nothing: it states which numbers no longer describe what ran, in the same posture as `deterministic: false`. The first implementation task is to record a reply's `model` into a committed file, which turns the constant into something a reader can check.
why: Grounding pass k1: the constant `typesafe/jev-1.13.0` has no witness anywhere in the pinned worktree, so the design proposes to hard-code a value nothing can check. Stated plainly as the design's weakest point, and turned into a concrete first implementation task rather than left as a caveat.

prop: Decision — routing and credential. A model value whose vendor half is exactly `typesafe` is sent to TypeSafe's endpoint (a second constant beside `ENDPOINT`, https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone) with a credential read only from the environment variable TYPESAFE_API_KEY, on the same terms `KEY_VARS` states for OpenRouter's: never a config key, never written. The refusal closes the path completely, but not for the reason an earlier draft gave. It is not that a config-file value evades the check: `accepted()` is applied in `resolve()` on every read, not only in `set()`, so a hand-edited `verify.model = typesafe/jev-1.13.0` is skipped on the way to a mint just as a `config set` of it is rejected at the prompt. The defect is in what the author is then told. `verify_model()` returns `resolve(...).0` and throws the `Source` away, so the rejection becomes an absence: `settings.model` is `None`, the status is `unauthorized`, and `block()`'s `missing` diagnostic says "`verify.model` is not set — `tetel config verify.model <vendor/model>`" to an author looking at a file where it plainly is set, and who will set it again to the same value. So the `missing` diagnostic gains an arm for the rejected case, fed by `config::rejections()` — which exists for exactly this, whose own doc comment states the rule that "a value it failed to apply must not be discoverable only by noticing the output looks wrong", and which no caller on the verify path uses today. That arm names the scope and the rejected value, and says the check leg cannot be a typed model.

The decision survives; its stated reason and its diagnostic do not.

prop: Decision — one new key, `verify.typed_model`, not a `verify.provider` and not one key per leg. A provider key would describe a switch that cannot exist: whatever it is set to, the check leg stays on OpenRouter. One key per leg would each have to be printed in every response and each have to earn its place, for legs that never run apart from a per-verb table. Set to a `typesafe/` value, it enables the typed legs that a per-verb table in source names for each verb — the same status `classify_system_for` already gives the classify prompt — and a response whose verification ran a typed leg carries `typed_model`, beside the version the endpoint resolved it to. The key is added the way `block()` adds an optional key and not the way it adds a mandatory one: through `map.insert` after the `json!` literal, which is how `for_mint`, `findings`, `literals_incomplete`, `queued_for` and `detail` are all emitted, so it is absent rather than null when no typed leg ran. That is what keeps it consistent with the invariant below rather than in tension with it — an unconditional key in the literal would change every response's field set, including those of a verifier no author asked to change. What is byte-identical to today is the verifier with no `typesafe/` value on any verify key, not merely with `typed_model` unset: `verify.refuter_model` accepts a `typesafe/` value today, because `is_model_name` has no vendor allowlist and `KEYS` gives that key `Accepts::ModelNameOrOff`, and routing follows the model value's vendor half wherever the value came from. `typed_model` unset with a `typesafe/` refuter set is a typed leg, and the per-verb table governs it as one.
why: Attack pass a2: "every response prints it as `typed_model`" and C22(1)'s "prints the same fields as today" cannot both hold literally. F20 settles which mechanism block() uses for an optional key — `map.insert`, not the object literal — so the claim can now name it instead of leaving the response shape undecided.

prop: Decision — what the gate does to a verification. The gate asks its question first, of the subject's text and evidence alone, before any classify call, which is how it was measured. prop: Decision — a typed leg's cost is priced in source, not left at zero. This design is sold on cost, and the mechanism that reports cost cannot see a typed call. `tel.cost` accumulates `v["usage"]["cost"]` from the provider's own envelope, defaulting to zero under a comment saying it is "Whatever the provider says it charged" and is "Absent on providers that report none". TypeSafe is such a provider: its reply carries `input_tokens` and no cost, which is why every Jev figure in this memo is priced by the harness instead — scripts/verifier-eval/jev.py records the published rate of $0.042 per million input tokens in its own header, defines `USD_PER_INPUT_TOKEN = 0.042 / 1_000_000`, and computes `cost = usage.get("input_tokens", 0) * USD_PER_INPUT_TOKEN`. Shipped as it stands, every typed leg would contribute exactly 0.00 to `Record.cost`, and `report_text`'s "cost — total, each" line would report a mint that made a gate call and a refuter call as having spent what the LLM legs alone spent. That is wrong in the direction that flatters this design: the savings it claims would be invisible in the one place a reader looks for them, and a workspace that ran typed legs and no LLM legs at all would report zero. So the input rate ships as a constant beside the endpoint constant, and a typed call is priced from the `input_tokens` its reply carries, by the same arithmetic jev.py already performs. This inherits the weakness C17 names for the version constant, and inherits it more sharply: a published price is a number that lives outside the tree, changes without notice, and — unlike the resolved model version — is not echoed in any reply, so nothing in a response can ever detect that it has drifted. The constant therefore carries the date it was read, and a typed leg's cost is documented as computed from a rate rather than reported by the provider. Leaving it at zero and documenting that instead was considered and rejected: a zero cost is indistinguishable from a leg that did not run, and this design's whole argument is arithmetic about what the legs cost.

prop: Decision — a typed leg's cost is priced in source, not left at zero. This design is sold on cost, and the mechanism that reports cost cannot see a typed call. `tel.cost` accumulates `v["usage"]["cost"]` from the provider's own envelope, in exactly one place, defaulting to zero under a comment saying it is "Whatever the provider says it charged" and is "Absent on providers that report none". TypeSafe is such a provider: the reply this memo's live call received carried `input_tokens` and no cost. That premise is weaker than the mechanism it supports, and weak in the way this memo's other version-and-shape claims are weak: no harness stores a raw response, `jev.ask()` keeps only `answers` and `usage`, so nothing on disk can confirm it and no grounding pass has. What the tree does show is consistent with it and hard to explain otherwise — scripts/verifier-eval/jev.py prices every Jev figure locally, recording the published rate in its own header as "input $0.042/MTok, output free", defining `USD_PER_INPUT_TOKEN = 0.042 / 1_000_000`, and computing `cost = usage.get("input_tokens", 0) * USD_PER_INPUT_TOKEN`, which is work nobody does against a provider that reports a price. That is wrong in the direction that flatters this design: the savings it claims would be invisible in the one place a reader looks for them, and a workspace that ran typed legs and no LLM legs at all would report zero. So the input rate ships as a constant beside the endpoint constant, and a typed call is priced from the `input_tokens` its reply carries, by the same arithmetic jev.py already performs. Pricing from input alone is complete rather than partial only because output is free at that published rate, and the constant carries that condition with it: a rate that began charging for output would make this arithmetic undercount in the same flattering direction, and the reply does carry `output_tokens` to multiply if it ever does. The constant therefore carries the date it was read, which is something the harness it is taken from does not record, so the date comes from this memo rather than from jev.py; and a typed leg's cost is documented as computed from a rate rather than reported by the provider. Leaving it at zero and documenting that instead was considered and rejected: a zero cost is indistinguishable from a leg that did not run, and this design's whole argument is arithmetic about what the legs cost. prop: Decision — a typed leg's cost is priced in source, not left at zero. This design is sold on cost, and the mechanism that reports cost cannot see a typed call. `tel.cost` accumulates `v["usage"]["cost"]` from the provider's own envelope, in exactly one place, defaulting to zero under a comment saying it is "Whatever the provider says it charged" and is "Absent on providers that report none". TypeSafe is such a provider, and two committed files show it. scripts/verifier-eval/jev_reply_2026-09-21.json keeps one reply whole, written unaltered by record_reply.py: its three top-level keys are `model`, `answers` and `usage`, and `usage` is {"input_tokens": 370, "output_tokens": 54} — two keys, no `cost`, and no cost anywhere else in the envelope. A benchmark file agrees for a different request: scripts/verifier-eval/fact_refuted_jev.json, at records[1].findings[0].refutation, carries `usage` = {'input_tokens': 3332, 'output_tokens': 61}, passed through by `jev.ask()`, which keeps `answers` and `usage` and composes neither. The tree's other behaviour is consistent: scripts/verifier-eval/jev.py prices every Jev figure locally, recording the published rate in its own header as "input $0.042/MTok, output free", defining `USD_PER_INPUT_TOKEN = 0.042 / 1_000_000`, and computing `cost = usage.get("input_tokens", 0) * USD_PER_INPUT_TOKEN`. Shipped without pricing, every typed leg would contribute exactly 0.00 to `Record.cost`, and `report_text`'s "cost — total, each" line would report a mint that made a gate call and a refuter call as having spent what the LLM legs alone spent. That is wrong in the direction that flatters this design: the savings it claims would be invisible in the one place a reader looks for them, and a workspace that ran typed legs and no LLM legs at all would report zero. Pricing from input alone is complete rather than partial only because output is free at that published rate, and the constant carries that condition with it: a rate that began charging for output would make this arithmetic undercount in the same flattering direction, and the reply does carry `output_tokens` to multiply if it ever does — both stored usage objects show that field present, so the undercount would be silent rather than visibly absent. The constant therefore carries the date it was read, which is something the harness it is taken from does not record, so the date comes from this memo rather than from jev.py; and a typed leg's cost is documented as computed from a rate rather than reported by the provider. Leaving it at zero and documenting that instead was considered and rejected: a zero cost is indistinguishable from a leg that did not run, and this design's whole argument is arithmetic about what the legs cost.
